Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- In keeping with President Obama's pledge of an administration that is "transparent and accountable," the White House has launched a site that promises to show taxpayers where their stimulus-package dollars are being spent. Visitors to Recovery.gov are greeted with a video message from President Obama. The site, Recovery.gov, allows visitors to track efforts to jump-start a teetering economy in the midst of a slumping housing market and massive job losses. It breaks down the $787 billion package by category: $288 billion for tax relief, $59 billion for health care, and so on. The site promises that more detailed spending information will be posted once federal agencies decide how they are going to allocate the money.  Learn more about where the money is going » . Using graphs, charts and layman's terminology, the online portal is an example of how the tech-savvy Obama administration is taking its message to the American people. While running for president, Obama harnessed the Web's fundraising and social-networking capabilities to energize his grass-roots campaign. And the moment he was sworn in as the 44th president of the United States, administration officials unveiled a sleek interactive version of Whitehouse.gov, the official White House Web site. Recovery.gov, launched within hours of Obama's signing of the stimulus bill Tuesday, continues the theme of offering information in a user-friendly format. Visitors are greeted by a brief video address from Obama. "The American Recovery and Reinvestment Plan represents a strategic and significant investment in our country's future," the president explains. "The size and scale of this plan demand unprecedented efforts to root out waste, inefficiency and unnecessary spending. Recovery.gov will be the online portal for these efforts." The site will publish information on how the stimulus funds will be spent in a "timely, targeted and transparent manner," Obama said. Edward Glaeser, a professor of economics at Harvard University, said transparency has "been a watch word for good government types for years." "There is sense that taxpayers will feel a lot better about this if they actually know where their money is going," Glaeser said. "Better transparency makes evaluation much easier." Glaeser pointed out that the idea behind Recovery.gov is not entirely new. He noted that the Office of Management and Budget has for years had a site where citizens can learn the available cost-benefit information of several government programs. Clicking on "Where is Your Money Going" on the new site brings up a chart displaying key areas where the $787 billion will be distributed, including tax relief, energy, health care and infrastructure and science. Under "Accountability and Transparency," there is a statement that reads, "This is your money. You have a right to know where it's going and how it's being spent. Learn what steps we're taking to ensure you can track our progress every step of the way." Like other Obama online portals, the site encourages user interaction. The public is invited to share stories on how the Recovery Act is affecting them. Scrolling over a map of the United States reveals data on the number of jobs created and saved in each state. Those with some time on their hands can also read, in its entirety, the full text of the legislation.

# White House Launches Recovery.gov to Track Stimulus Spending

The White House has launched Recovery.gov, a new website designed to fulfill President Obama's campaign pledge of running a "transparent and accountable" administration. The site aims to give American taxpayers a clear window into how the government is spending funds from the massive economic stimulus package, allowing citizens to track where their tax dollars are going in real time.

## Breaking Down the $787 Billion Package

Recovery.gov organizes the sprawling $787 billion stimulus package into digestible categories, making the complex legislation more accessible to ordinary Americans. Among the largest allocations highlighted on the site are $288 billion designated for tax relief and $59 billion earmarked for health care initiatives. Rather than presenting this information as dense legislative text, the site employs graphs, charts, and other visual aids to explain the spending in straightforward, layman's terms—an approach intended to demystify how the stimulus funds will flow through the economy.

## Promise of Greater Detail to Come

While the current version of the site provides a broad overview of spending categories, the administration has promised that more granular information will follow. As federal agencies work out the specifics of how they will allocate their portions of the stimulus funds, Recovery.gov is expected to be updated with increasingly detailed breakdowns, giving the public a more precise picture of where the money is being directed.

## Part of a Broader Digital Strategy

The launch of Recovery.gov is emblematic of the tech-savvy Obama administration's broader strategy of leveraging the internet to communicate directly with the American public, bypassing traditional media filters when possible. This approach builds on the digital tactics that proved successful during Obama's presidential campaign, as well as the administration's revamped Whitehouse.gov website, which has similarly emphasized transparency and direct citizen engagement since Obama took office.

## Obama's Message on Accountability

In a video message posted directly on the Recovery.gov site, President Obama underscored the unprecedented scale of the challenge at hand. He emphasized that the sheer size of the recovery plan demands extraordinary efforts to root out waste, fraud, and inefficiency in how the funds are spent. Obama pledged that information about stimulus spending would be published in what he described as a "timely, targeted and transparent manner," reinforcing the administration's commitment to accountability as it moves forward with implementing the historic economic recovery package.

# New Website Aims to Track Stimulus Spending as Obama Pushes Government Transparency

WASHINGTON (CNN) — The Obama administration launched Recovery.gov on Thursday, a website designed to let taxpayers track how the $787 billion economic stimulus package is being spent, marking what officials call a major step in the president's promise to run the most transparent administration in American history.

The website allows users to search for stimulus spending by state, congressional district, and federal agency, showing where contracts, grants, and loans are being awarded. Officials say the site will eventually include maps and searchable databases that break down funding all the way to the local level.

"The American people have a right to know where their tax dollars are going and how they're being spent," said Earl Devaney, chairman of the Recovery Accountability and Transparency Board, the independent panel overseeing the site. "This is about accountability, plain and simple."

The launch comes as the administration faces mounting scrutiny over how quickly stimulus funds are reaching states and whether the spending is creating the jobs officials promised. Republican critics have questioned both the pace of the rollout and the effectiveness of the spending itself, with some lawmakers calling for more oversight before additional funds are released.

Vice President Joe Biden, who has been tasked with overseeing stimulus implementation, said the website would help combat waste and fraud by putting the information directly in the hands of citizens and watchdog groups.

"Sunlight is still the best disinfectant," Biden said in a statement. "If federal money is being spent badly, we want to hear about it — and so should you."

The site is part of a broader transparency push the president outlined during his first days in office, when he signed a memorandum directing federal agencies to embrace openness and use technology to make government data more accessible. Obama has repeatedly pledged that his administration would operate differently from previous ones, promising to post bills online before signing them and to make government spending easier for ordinary citizens to track.

Government watchdog groups offered cautious praise for the new site, saying the intent was good but that the true test would be whether the data proves accurate and timely.

"A website is only as good as the information behind it," said Gary Bass, executive director of OMB Watch, a nonprofit that monitors federal spending. "If agencies are slow to report or the numbers don't add up, this could backfire and undermine the credibility the administration is trying to build."

Some state officials have also raised concerns about the reporting burden the site places on local governments, which are required to submit detailed data on how stimulus funds are being used in their communities. Several have said they are still working out how to comply with the reporting requirements ahead of looming deadlines.

Despite the challenges, White House officials say Recovery.gov represents just the beginning of a broader effort to overhaul how the federal government interacts with the public. Additional initiatives, including a rework of the Freedom of Information Act process and new open-data standards for federal agencies, are expected to follow in the coming months.

"This is a new way of doing business in Washington," said White House Press Secretary Robert Gibbs. "We're not going to get it perfect on day one, but the president is committed to making sure this information keeps improving and keeps growing."

The website's launch drew immediate traffic, with users reporting sporadic slowdowns Thursday afternoon as visitors flooded the site to search stimulus data in their own states and districts.

The administration has said it will continue updating Recovery.gov as more contracts are awarded and more state and local reports come in, with plans to add more robust search tools and data visualizations in the coming weeks.

Recovery.gov was created in response to public demand for accountability following passage of the stimulus package, which was intended to jumpstart the economy through infrastructure investment, tax relief, and expanded social programs during the recession. # Recovery.gov: The Website That Tried to Make Washington Show Its Work

When Congress passed the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act in February 2009, pumping roughly $787 billion into the economy amid the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression, lawmakers faced an immediate credibility problem. How would taxpayers know where the money actually went?

The answer was Recovery.gov, an ambitious—and at the time unprecedented—federal website designed to track stimulus spending down to the county level. It represented one of the first large-scale experiments in using the internet to create real-time government accountability, requiring recipients of federal contracts, grants, and loans to report quarterly on how funds were being used and how many jobs were being created or saved.

The site allowed users to search by state, zip code, or congressional district, producing maps and charts that broke down spending across categories like infrastructure, education, energy, and healthcare. For a government more accustomed to burying spending data in dense budget documents, it was a notable shift toward radical transparency.

## Why It Mattered

The stakes went beyond simple bookkeeping. With public trust in government already fragile, the Obama administration billed Recovery.gov as a tool to prevent the waste, fraud, and abuse that had plagued previous federal spending programs. An independent oversight board, the Recovery Accountability and Transparency Board, was created specifically to manage the site and investigate reporting discrepancies.

Economists watching the rollout saw it as significant for reasons that extended well past the stimulus itself.

"What Recovery.gov represented wasn't just a website—it was a test case for whether democratic governments could use transparency as a genuine check on spending, rather than as a public relations exercise," said one economist who studies public finance and government accountability. "Historically, the biggest obstacle to identifying wasteful spending has been the sheer opacity of the process. If you can show citizens, in near real-time, where a contract went and whether the promised jobs materialized, you fundamentally change the incentive structure for public officials and contractors alike."

That accountability function proved complicated in practice. Early data on job creation numbers drew scrutiny for inconsistencies—some reports listed jobs in congressional districts that didn't exist, and job-creation figures were sometimes overstated or miscalculated by recipients unfamiliar with reporting requirements. The Recovery board acknowledged these errors and worked to correct them, arguing that the mistakes reflected growing pains in an enormous, novel reporting system rather than deliberate fraud.

## A Template for the Future

Still, many observers argued that Recovery.gov's importance lay less in perfect execution and more in establishing a template. The site pushed forward standards for open data formats, machine-readable spending information, and public dashboards that would influence later transparency initiatives, including USASpending.gov and subsequent efforts to modernize federal financial reporting.

"Transparency tools rarely work perfectly on the first try," the economist noted. "The real test is whether the system self-corrects and whether it changes public expectations going forward. Once citizens have tasted the ability to see where their tax dollars go, it becomes very difficult for future administrations to roll that back without facing real political cost."

In that sense, Recovery.gov's legacy may be less about the specific dollars it tracked during the 2009 stimulus and more about the precedent it set: that in the digital age, government spending—even spending measured in hundreds of billions of dollars—could no longer hide behind bureaucratic complexity alone.

# White House Launches Recovery.gov to Track Stimulus Fund Allocation

**WASHINGTON, D.C.** — The federal government unveiled a new website this week designed to give Americans unprecedented visibility into how funds from the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act are being distributed and spent across the country.

The website, Recovery.gov, allows users to track stimulus spending by state, congressional district, and federal agency, marking what officials describe as an ambitious effort toward government transparency and accountability.

## A New Era of Transparency

In an introductory video message posted to the site, President Obama emphasized the administration's commitment to ensuring taxpayers can see exactly where their money is going.

"This is your money, and you deserve to know where it's going and how it's being spent," Obama said in the video. "That's why I'm committed to making sure the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act is implemented with an unprecedented level of transparency and accountability."

The President noted that the scale of the recovery effort—hundreds of billions of dollars directed toward infrastructure, education, healthcare, and clean energy projects—demanded a new level of public oversight.

"We don't just need a government that spends wisely and invests these precious dollars efficiently," he continued. "We need a government that's open and honest with the American people about how this money is spent."

## How the Website Works

Recovery.gov features interactive maps and searchable databases that allow visitors to see:

- The amount of stimulus funding allocated to their state
- Specific projects funded through the Recovery Act
- Job creation estimates tied to funded projects
- Reports from recipients on fund usage

Officials say the site will be updated regularly as more data becomes available from federal agencies and state governments, with the ultimate goal of tracking funds down to the local level.

## Oversight and Accountability

The website is overseen by the Recovery Accountability and Transparency Board, an independent body created specifically to monitor stimulus spending and guard against fraud, waste, and abuse.

Obama addressed concerns about mismanagement directly in his message, stating that his administration would hold agencies accountable for how funds are used.

"We're not going to tolerate any surprises," he said, adding that inspectors general and oversight committees would play an active role in monitoring implementation.

## Public Reaction

The launch has drawn mixed reactions from lawmakers and watchdog groups. Supporters have praised the initiative as a meaningful step toward restoring public trust in government spending, particularly amid concerns about the size and speed of the stimulus rollout. Critics, however, have questioned whether the site will provide sufficiently detailed or timely data to allow for real accountability.

Despite the debate, the administration has framed Recovery.gov as a living project—one that will evolve based on public feedback and technological improvements.

"We want citizens to be able to hold us accountable," Obama said in closing his remarks. "This is your recovery, and this is your government."
